utterances.text: Does it mean that Fatmir Kamberi and your son, Rami, were not close friends, or were not friends at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not friends. I have never seen Rami speaking to him. He was involved in other business. He mainly worked in the town, while my son was mainly engaged in agriculture. I don't know what else to state about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Was maybe Fatmir Kamberi in your yard on Saturday evening towards the Sunday?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we may enter a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: You said that the electricity went off in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: When did your wife start preparing the breakfast?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: She started preparing the breakfast when there was still electricity, and as soon as electricity went off, she stopped. We didn't have any proper breakfast. We just had something to eat, just some bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that you had a gas stove as an alternative in your house?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A three- or five-litre one; I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you have breakfast on Sunday morning?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: In the statement of 22nd of April, 2007, 2D 2253, page 3, paragraph 5, she said that she took you back from the gate to have a breakfast, but actually you didn't have breakfast that day. Will you agree with me for this being correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even nowadays I don't eat breakfast. I almost never have breakfast. She did take a crust of bread and ate it. Now, don't ask me what exactly we had for breakfast because this is not related to the matters we discuss here. She took a crust of bread in the kitchen and ate it. The younger people, they get up later on and they eat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In the consolidated statement of yours, 2 2D 71, paragraph 21, you say that: "I had breakfast in the corridor." In the addendum -- or correction to the 92 ter rule is a statement of Elmaz Jusufi of 22nd of April, 2007, 2D 2295, page 4, paragraph 15, you say that: "Between 7.30 and 8.00, I returned to the house and had breakfast in the corridor." These are your statements given before the ICTY OTP investigators. Could you tell us what is correct now?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I'm in a wheelchair, and do you want me to tell you how I eat? I take a piece of bread, I eat it with some salt. For me, this is normal. I'm -- may eat only five or six grams of bread during the day. That's why I'm in the state I am now. I'm really confused why you're asking me these questions. Ask me where it hurts, where the core matter lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: I would go back again to the moment of the death of your son. I really feel sorry, but I think that this question had to be asked and I would ask a few more questions regarding this event, bearing in mind that my colleague Edina elaborated this in detail. I would ask just a few, and I would repeat brief questions.

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: When your son was hit, what was his position in relation to the door? We are talking about the door that is an entrance to your home.

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain it to you in practical terms. Here is the hand. He caught the door in order to close it. He was turned like this. This was his position. If I could demonstrate it to you, I would have done it properly, but he just grabbed the handle. He turned like this and fell on the ground. This is very clear. If we were there in the house and if I was in a better state, I would have explained it exactly, how he was standing in relation to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Jusufi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt and try and include on the record what I gathered of that demonstration, that Mr. Jusufi stood, as I understood it, facing the open doorway, reached out with his left hand to demonstrate grasping the door, and then swung with his body to his right, and as he turned, he indicated his son was hit. I -- that is what I could make of the demonstration. Is that what you had in mind, Mr. Jusufi, and what you were trying to show to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. His stomach was opposite to the policemen, turned towards the policemen, and as the door was opened ajar, his hand was like this, so he was like this, in front of the policemen. And this was the moment when he was shot and fell down. The bullet caught him badly. As soon as he fell down, he said, "They killed me." We thought that it was not a major wound, but it turned out that it was. This was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From what I saw then, Mr. Jusufi indicated that his son was standing with his stomach facing the open door, and then as his left hand grasped the door and he turned to the right, there was a firing and the bullet caught him. You want to ask more about that, Mr. Apostolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Once your son --

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, should we go to a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm trying to judge Mr. Jusufi's condition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. If you are not planning a break now, we can go on. Don't do it just because of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd like to try and finish your questions before we have a break, Mr. Apostolski, because we have to set up the courtroom for a different type of witness, you see, during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I will finish my questions in the course of today. I don't believe I will be able to finalise my questions before the break, but by the end of the day, I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm assuming from what you said earlier, you might have five or ten minutes more questioning, Mr. Apostolski; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I will need 20 to 25 more minutes, with all due respect to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being the case, we will have a break now for everybody's sake, and we will resume at 6.00. --- Upon recessing at 5.28 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufi, I will ask you a few more brief questions in order to finish your testimony as soon as possible. After your son was wounded, did you call anyone?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't have a telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you besides your son all the time after he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We stayed by his side all day. We were kind of -- we felt paralysed, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: How soon after the wounding your son died?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise time. Maybe after half an hour or 40 minutes, 25 minutes. I wouldn't be able to say. I know it wasn't long after he was wounded. Not more than, let's say, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufi, can we then conclude that it is correct in your opinion that it was at the most 40 minutes, 45 minutes after the wounding that your son died?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 45, you said? As I said, I can't be -- can't be precise. We were very -- we were horrified at his death. We didn't even look at the clock. More or less.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did your son talk to someone else, apart from the three of you inside the house?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't talk with us either, because he fell down on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: So your son was not able, he was not in a condition to phone anyone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. That's correct. As I told you, we didn't even have a phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the names of the Albanian MPs in the Macedonian assembly, or at least any of them?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know all of them, not only the Albanians. I know all the MPs. But I don't think it's a proper time to mention their names. Arben Xhaferi is a member of the Parliament. Menduh Thaqi is also an MP. Matoshi is another one. And I can tell you the Macedonian names, but you can see them all the time on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: No, no. Is it correct that Mr. Fatmir Etemi was an MP in the Macedonian assembly?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was before. In 2002, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: During the period 10th to 12th of August, 2001, was Mr. Fatmir Etemi an MP in the Macedonian assembly?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Does he, as an MP, safeguard the interests of the Albanians in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much he stood up for them. He would look after his own interests, but what you're saying is normal, he should do that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you think that he would say something incorrect with regards to the Ljuboten case?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might say what -- he might say what might not be true. I don't know. He might say things which are based on hearsay. I know that he came up to the police check-point but turned back because he couldn't make it any further. He couldn't come and see the people who were in Kodrozemi [phoen]. I heard this from other co-villagers. How true that is, you may know better.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Whether you and Mr. Fatmir Etemi have spoken about the death of your son?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came after my son's death, Fatmir Etemi came, and Muarem Jusufi, they came to pay me a visit, came to the village, stayed for half an hour and left. Yes, they did come. But I didn't know them personally, but they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: I would read to you the statement of (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would move for a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did the Macedonian security forces -- I apologise. Did the Macedonian security forces enter your house?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It seems that in the past with this witness -- with this particular witness, the phrase "inside your house" or "entering your house," could have more than one meaning, because as we've seen from the photographs, there was a large gate near the road and then, of course, below that, there was the home itself. And I'm wondering whether my colleague could be a bit more specific about what he's asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that there is reason to be a little more careful, Mr. Apostolski, because we've had difficulty in understanding this issue earlier in the day. You're asking, are you, whether there were police or Macedonian security personnel inside the yard of the house or inside the front door of the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I'm speaking about the house, I am speaking about the place where Mr. Rami Jusufi lives. When I'm asking another question, then I'm asking about the yard. So from now onwards, I will be more specific and I will say "inside the house where Mr. Rami Jusufi lives."

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you, Mr. Rami Jusufi -- I apologise. Did, Mr. Jusufi, Macedonian security forces enter the house where you live?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not enter inside my house. They came up to the yard and up to the door, the entrance door to my house. They came so far. And then when they kicked the door --

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you injured by any of the security forces?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't. They saw me, but they didn't do anything to me. I cannot say that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did anyone injure your wife?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: One more, the last question, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufi, can you confirm that you have stated that you have seen a helicopter flying over the village on the Sunday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it, yes, one helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusufi. I apologise for having to examine you, but these questions were going towards asserting the real truth about the events in Ljuboten, the real truth about the -- the situation where your son was injured and how did he die, and I think that this question and this Court will establish properly the factual situation and then the justice will be determined properly. Thank you, Mr. Jusufi, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe this will only take a few minutes, Your Honour. Before I begin, I would like to ask the usher if he could lower the arm of the ELMO, because it is impossible for Mr. Jusufi and I to look at each other. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufi, earlier this afternoon when my colleague Mr. Apostolski began to ask you some questions, he asked you some questions about politics in Macedonia. He asked you whether, for example, members of the Albanian community could vote freely. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You've lived in Macedonia your entire life; right?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, has there ever been an ethnic Albanian president of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During Communism, yes. Not president, but deputy chairman of Macedonia, Starova. But during democracy, no, we didn't have a president or - how you call that? - the head of the government, president of the government, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The democratic period then since 1991 or 1992, has there ever been an ethnic Albanian prime minister of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why do you suppose that is?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say? We are a minority in Macedonia and usually it's the majority that forms the government. The prime minister comes out of this majority. I don't know how to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There was an exhibit that was admitted yesterday, I believe during Ms. Residovic's cross-examination. That was Exhibit D 23. Could that be shown to the witness, please, or pulled up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think D 23 can be correct, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask the witness to correct it. I'm simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, no, the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Really. It was 65 ter number 170, page 5. It is -- I believe at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it 2D 3, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please. It's interesting, at page 40 of the LiveNote the number in the transcript from yesterday is 23, Your Honour. I apologise if I'm creating confusion. Perhaps you're right. Perhaps it's 2D 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think either number is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist a little bit further. If -- I will use the Prosecution's exhibit number to save time. This would be 65 ter number 170 and the fifth page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be 1D 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that number in the transcript. But according to the transcript that appears to come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it was tendered by Ms. Residovic, it is 1D because that is first Defence. 2D is second Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So this -- I believe there is 1D 3, Your Honour, and I'm grateful to Ms. Walpita for clarifying this. But I can use this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufi, yesterday when Ms. Residovic showed you this photograph, she pointed out to you sort of the frame of a window on the left-hand side of the photograph; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see where you marked the number 1? Do you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To the right of that number 1, there's some marks on the wall, and you made a comment about them yesterday. And this is at page 38, the first few lines of the LiveNote transcript. Yesterday, you said this: "This is the mark that was hit by the police and I have not changed it. I keep it that way." Can you help us, please. What hit that wall; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the mark left by the bullets. They -- they shot also inside the room. That's not the only one. All the glasses of the windows were broken. The bullets entered inside the rooms. This is only outside. There were a lot of bullets that were fired. Their -- Honourable Judges, you should know that after they killed my son, they fired many bursts of fire, thousands of bullets, I would say. I left that one, but you can see holes in the frames as well. You can see holes are still there, because the bullets hit not only the glass but also the window frame. The stairs is made up of strong material, and even there you can see bullets that have hit it and have destroyed the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ELMAZ JUSUFI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I took a long time; I apologise for going into more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Jusufi, you will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give. We know it has been difficult physically and emotionally for you. And we would now indicate that the court officer will help you to leave the courtroom and that you may of course now go with your wife back to your home as soon as the arrangements can be made. It will be some little time, I'm afraid, before we finish all the evidence, but you will just have to wait in patience for the end of the case to see what might be the outcome. But we would like to thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, Your Honours, for making it possible for me to come here and tell you the truth as it was, because I know that this is the highest Tribunal in the world which has been approved by the Security Council to judge serious crimes. Therefore, I want to extend my thanks to you, Your Honours, for enabling me to come here and tell you the truth. Otherwise, I wouldn't be here. I wouldn't have come here if I were not to tell the truth. I want to thank you very much again, and I'm very pleased with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusufi. The court officer will help you now to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening to all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saxon, in view of the hour, and the fact that we needed 20 minutes to set up the courtroom for the next witness, we have already, through the court staff, made arrangements for that witness to leave and to be back here at 2.15 tomorrow. There was just no way that we could get any practical time out of the evidence that witness could give if we were to start at five minutes to 7.00. But at the commencement of today, you indicated there was a matter you wished to raise, so can we deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and this should only take a few moments of the Court's time. I would like to raise a matter related to witness scheduling. First of all, the Prosecution filed a motion today -- actually, before I go any further, are we in public or private session? I apologise for not keeping track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May we please go into private session, because this -- we need to discuss the situation of one or more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber would indicate that it is already very concerned at the rate of progress or lack of it in dealing with the evidence. When the Prosecution opened, it was brave enough to venture the possibility that we could finish the Prosecution case in perhaps 11 weeks or certainly three months. On present progress, if we maintain that rate, the most pessimistic view is that we would still be hearing the Prosecution evidence at the beginning of next year. That's how dramatically wrong our progress has been so far. Now, the Chamber is well aware that we are just starting into a new case with new procedures, and that it will take time for all counsel to adjust. In the Chamber's view, it is time for us to encourage you to take particular attention to that. Yes, for the Prosecution, if you have a witness whose evidence is essentially given in the form of a written statement, the extra questions asked need to be looked at to see whether they really are important and relevant. For the Defence, both Defence teams, it's very important that you come to a clear view very early in the case, we would suggest, as to what matters are important to your Defence and what matters are just incidental. If your proposition, for example, is that a witness has made a number of statements that conflict with evidence given here, it is more than enough to illustrate that by putting to the witness important differences. There's no need to track down every little discrepancy. There are some things that matter, and there are other things that we can all be confused or mistaken about. If it is going to have significant weight with the Chamber, it is likely to need to be one of those important matters that the witness has differed about. So that if you concentrate on those, we will not unnecessarily waste time, and you will be able to make the point that is important for your client and make it the more effectively if it can be made quickly with a few very clear examples over matters that are really important. Secondly, we can already see, and I'm sure you've realised yourself, that you have gone away and each prepared separately to cross-examine the same witness, with the result that often the same issues are put to the witness twice, questions are really repetitive. Now, once the matter has been aired, there is no need to go over it again. It's there, the witness has told you the answer to the issue that you're going to put. So we would encourage counsel to be very conscious of these matters -- I'm looking for the microphone that's on somewhere, we're getting feedback, but I can't see it, apart from mine. That feedback sound is normally an indication that there is a second microphone switched on, but we will carry on. It's important that you try and concentrate on the issues that matter and avoid merely duplicating points that have already been put to the witness and dealt with. And a second proposition that you might care to consider is that if a witness has said, "I was at so-and-so on" -- I'll give something that is nothing to do with this case, "on the morning of 9th of May, 2007." If the witness has said that, it's on the transcript, we've heard it, we know it. There's no value in saying, "Now, you have said in this Court that you were at so-and-so on the 9th of May, 2007, is that correct," before going on to put to him that he said some other time that he was not there on that day, or to put to him that other witnesses will say that he wasn't there, he was at a very different place. So there's no need just to get confirmation of what he has already said, it's there, it's in the record, it's clear that he has said it. The point you want to make is that he said something quite different at some other time, or that other witnesses will say something quite different, and correctly that's put to him to see whether he has some explanation for the difference or not. You will understand that these matters are offered by the Chamber as a way of trying to assist counsel as quickly as possible to get into the way of our procedure here and to speed up the rate at which we are dealing with what really matters in this case, because if we can't achieve that, all of us will be here for very much longer than expected, and what is important for the Defence is that it means the two accused and their families will be waiting a very much longer time to come to the end of the case and to get the outcome. And they, of course, have a very significant interest in having their case properly heard, but properly heard as quickly as possible. So we would encourage you with those things, and you will understand that we may have to offer some further comments as we gain more experience over the next few days and even weeks. You will be aware that in some cases, some Trial Chambers find they really must, in the end, impose time-limits to make sure that we keep within a strict time. Now, we prefer to avoid that, if we can, because we prefer to leave it to the judgement of counsel as to what is important and what isn't. We put that trust in counsel. We ask that it be respected by counsel really only spending time on those things that really matter to their case. With that, we can hear the case fairly and fully and as quickly as possible, which is our objective. It's time now to adjourn for the day. We resume tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of May, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.51 p.m.,
